title: Exercise 7A · Q11
summary: Find YX with Pythagoras, then YP from two expressions for the area of ΔWXY.
alt: Exercise 7A · Q11: In ΔWXY, WY = 24 m and ∠Y = 90°. P lies on WX such that YP is perpendicular to WX, WP = 18 m and PX = 14 m. Q lies on YX such that QX = 9.8 m. Find (i) the length of YQ, (ii) the area of ΔXPY.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: In **ΔWXY**, **WY = 24 m** and **∠Y = 90°**. **P** lies on **WX** such that **YP ⊥ WX**, **WP = 18 m** and **PX = 14 m**. **Q** lies on **YX** such that **QX = 9.8 m**. We have to find (i) **YQ** and (ii) the **area of ΔXPY**.

steps.title: Find WX
steps.narration: First add the two parts of the long side **WX**.\[\begin{aligned}WX &= WP + PX \\ &= 18 + 14 = 32\ \text{m}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔWXY, **∠Y = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **WX**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. We want a shorter side, so subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{WX^2} &= \role{legA}{WY^2} + \role{legB}{YX^2} \\ \role{legB}{YX^2} &= \role{hyp}{WX^2} - \role{legA}{WY^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and subtract
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{WX^2} &= \role{legA}{WY^2} + \role{legB}{YX^2} \\ \role{legB}{YX^2} &= \role{hyp}{WX^2} - \role{legA}{WY^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{32^2} - \role{legA}{24^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1024} - \role{legA}{576} \\ &= \role{legB}{448}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 448 is not a perfect square. Use a calculator and keep 4 significant figures — we need this value again.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{WX^2} &= \role{legA}{WY^2} + \role{legB}{YX^2} \\ \role{legB}{YX^2} &= \role{hyp}{WX^2} - \role{legA}{WY^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{32^2} - \role{legA}{24^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1024} - \role{legA}{576} \\ &= \role{legB}{448} \\ \role{legB}{YX} &= \sqrt{448} = 8\sqrt{7} = 21.17\ \text{m}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: (i) Find YQ
steps.narration: **YQ** is what is left of **YX** after taking away **QX**.\[\begin{aligned}YQ &= YX - QX \\ &= 21.17 - 9.8 \\ &= \role{ans}{11.4\ \text{m}}\ \text{(3 s.f.)}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: (ii) Two ways to find the area
steps.narration: To find the area of **ΔXPY** we need the height **YP**. Write the area of **ΔWXY** in two ways: using **Y** as the right angle, and using **YP** as the height.\[\begin{aligned}\text{Area of } \triangle WXY &= \tfrac{1}{2} \times WY \times YX \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2} \times WX \times YP\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Find YP
steps.narration: Make the two expressions equal and solve for **YP**.\[\begin{aligned}\tfrac{1}{2} \times WY \times YX &= \tfrac{1}{2} \times WX \times YP \\ YP &= \frac{24 \times 21.17}{32} \\ &= 15.9\ \text{m}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Area of ΔXPY
steps.narration: **ΔXPY** has a right angle at **P**, so its area is half base × height.\[\begin{aligned}\text{Area} &= \tfrac{1}{2} \times PX \times PY \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 14 \times 15.9 \\ &= \role{ans}{111\ \text{m}^2}\ \text{(3 s.f.)}\end{aligned}\]

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Check WX
challenges.prompt: WP = 18 m and PX = 14 m. How long is **WX**?

takeaways: A right-angled triangle's area can be written **two ways** — using the two shorter sides, or using the hypotenuse and its height.
Split the figure into right-angled triangles and solve them **one at a time**; each answer feeds the next triangle.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always begin with a line such as "In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. Using Pythagoras' Theorem," — it shows which triangle and which right angle you are using.

notes.title: Rounding
notes.text: If the answer is not a whole number, give it to **3 significant figures** unless the question says otherwise.
